noteBlocks.md: Some salts crystallise with water **chemically bonded into the crystal structure**: **water of crystallisation**. A salt holding it is **hydrated**; with it removed, the salt is **anhydrous**. The dot in a formula counts it.

**See it on washing soda**, $\ce{Na2CO3.10H2O}$:
**1.** The part after the dot gives 10 waters per $\ce{Na2CO3}$.
**2.** Heating to constant mass leaves $\ce{Na2CO3}$, the anhydrous salt.

noteBlocks.prompt: What is meant by the term hydrated?
options: contains water of crystallisation
dissolved in water
has had its water removed
noteBlocks.explain: A hydrated salt still holds the water bonded into its crystal, as washing soda holds its 10 waters. Dissolved describes a solution, and a salt with its water removed is anhydrous. Hydrated means it contains water of crystallisation.

noteBlocks.prompt: How many water molecules are bonded into the crystal for each MgSO₄ unit in MgSO₄·7H₂O?
noteBlocks.explain: Read the number after the dot, as step 1 did for washing soda: 7H₂O means 7 water molecules of crystallisation for every MgSO₄.

noteBlocks.alt: A bar for the relative formula mass of CuSO4.5H2O, 250, split into CuSO4, 160, and five waters of 18, 90.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="hybar"><title id="hybar">A bar for the relative formula mass of CuSO4 with 5 waters, 250, split into the anhydrous salt, 160, and 5 waters of 18 each, 90</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"><rect x="20" y="56" width="360" height="34" rx="3"/><path d="M250.4 56 L250.4 90"/><path d="M20 104 V112 H250.4 V104"/><path d="M250.4 104 V112 H380 V104"/></g><g font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor"><text x="20" y="30" font-size="14" text-anchor="start" font-weight="600">CuSO₄·5H₂O: Mr 250</text><text x="135.2" y="79" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">CuSO₄</text><text x="315.2" y="79" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">5H₂O</text><text x="135.2" y="132" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">160</text><text x="315.2" y="132" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">5 × 18 = 90</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: The hydrate's Mr is the salt's Mr plus the water's.

noteBlocks.md: Add the salt's Mr to the water's. Each $\ce{H2O}$ is $2 \times 1 + 16 = 18$, so n waters add $n \times 18$. Count every atom of the salt first: an oxygen left out cost many candidates the mark in 2025.

noteBlocks.title: Why the water counts in the Mr
noteBlocks.md: The water is part of the solid: every unit of the crystal carries its waters with it, so a mole of the hydrate weighs the salt plus all of them.

noteBlocks.prompt: Using Mg = 24, S = 32, O = 16 and H = 1, work out the Mr of MgSO₄·7H₂O.
noteBlocks.explain: Do what the steps did: the salt first, MgSO₄ = 24 + 32 + 4 × 16 = 120; then the water, 7 × 18 = 126; then add them: 246.

noteBlocks.text: 3. See it done: x from the Mr

noteBlocks.caption: Take the salt away; what is left is the water.

noteBlocks.md:
**The question** (2023 shape): hydrated copper(II) sulfate, $\ce{CuSO4.xH2O}$, has Mr 250. Find x. **[3]**
**Step 1.** $\ce{CuSO4}$: $64 + 32 + 4 \times 16 = 160$.
**Step 2.** The water: $250 - 160 = 90$.
**Step 3.** $x = 90 \div 18 = 5$.

noteBlocks.prompt: Hydrated cobalt(II) chloride, CoCl₂·xH₂O, has Mr 238. Using Co = 59 and Cl = 35.5, find x.
noteBlocks.explain: Follow the three steps: CoCl₂ = 59 + 2 × 35.5 = 130; the water is 238 − 130 = 108; and 108 ÷ 18 = 6. Stopping at 108 gives the water's mass, not x.

noteBlocks.alt: A crucible holding the hydrated salt rests in a pipeclay triangle on a tripod, heated from below by a Bunsen burner standing on a heatproof mat.

noteBlocks.md: Heat the hydrated salt in a crucible or an evaporating basin, let it cool, and weigh it. Then **heat, cool and weigh again**, repeating until **two weighings agree**: that is **constant mass**, and it shows all the water of crystallisation has gone. Driving water off by heating is a **thermal decomposition**.

**See the readings**, blue $\ce{CuSO4.5H2O}$ in a crucible:
**1.** Weigh the empty crucible, then add the salt: 18.42 g, then 20.92 g.
**2.** Heating, cooling and weighing 4 times gives 20.21, 20.05, 20.02, 20.02 g.
**3.** The last 2 readings agree, which makes 20.02 g the constant mass.

noteBlocks.prompt: Why is the crucible heated, cooled and weighed again and again until two masses are the same?
options: to make sure all the water of crystallisation has been removed
to let the crucible cool down
to check that the balance is working
noteBlocks.answer: to make sure all the water of crystallisation has been removed
noteBlocks.explain: While water is still leaving, each heating lowers the mass, as the readings fell from 20.21 g. Once two readings agree, nothing more can be driven off, so all the water of crystallisation has been removed.

noteBlocks.text: 5. See it done: the mass of water

noteBlocks.md:
**The three masses** a results table asks for:
**Hydrated salt:** 20.92 − 18.42 = 2.50 g.
**Anhydrous salt:** 20.02 − 18.42 = 1.60 g, from the constant mass.
**Water lost:** 2.50 − 1.60 = 0.90 g.
The blue crystals are now a white powder.

noteBlocks.prompt: A crucible weighs 21.30 g, with hydrated sodium carbonate 24.16 g, and 22.36 g at constant mass. What mass of water was lost, in g?
noteBlocks.explain: Take both masses from the crucible, as the three lines did: the hydrated salt is 24.16 − 21.30 = 2.86 g and the anhydrous salt 22.36 − 21.30 = 1.06 g, so the water is 2.86 − 1.06 = 1.80 g.

noteBlocks.alt: One MgSO4 unit beside seven water molecules: 0.02 mol of MgSO4 and 0.14 mol of water, a ratio of 1 to 7.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 170" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="hyrat"><title id="hyrat">One salt unit beside 7 water molecules: 0.02 mol of MgSO4 and 0.14 mol of water, a ratio of 1 to 7</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"><rect x="30" y="66" width="30" height="30" rx="3"/><circle cx="130" cy="70" r="11"/><circle cx="170" cy="70" r="11"/><circle cx="210" cy="70" r="11"/><circle cx="250" cy="70" r="11"/><circle cx="290" cy="70" r="11"/><circle cx="130" cy="104" r="11"/><circle cx="170" cy="104" r="11"/></g><g font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor"><text x="45" y="50" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600">MgSO₄</text><text x="210" y="40" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600">H₂O</text><text x="45" y="124" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">0.02 mol</text><text x="210" y="138" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">0.14 mol</text><text x="200" y="162" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">0.14 ÷ 0.02 = 7, so 1 : 7</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: x is a ratio of particles, so it comes from moles.

noteBlocks.md: The formula counts particles, so x is a **mole** ratio: the moles of water lost divided by the moles of anhydrous salt. Find each with moles = mass ÷ Mr; water's Mr is 18.

noteBlocks.title: Divide the moles
noteBlocks.md: Summer 2023's C2 Higher report: most found both numbers of moles, but very few went on to divide them to reach x.

noteBlocks.prompt: 7.15 g of hydrated sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃·xH₂O, leaves 2.65 g at constant mass. Using Mr(Na₂CO₃) = 106, find x.
noteBlocks.explain: The water is 7.15 − 2.65 = 4.50 g, which is 4.50 ÷ 18 = 0.25 mol. The salt is 2.65 ÷ 106 = 0.025 mol. Divide the water's moles by the salt's: 0.25 ÷ 0.025 = 10.

noteBlocks.text: 7. Why x uses moles, not masses

noteBlocks.caption: Nearly the same mass, very different numbers of particles.

noteBlocks.md: Equal masses are not equal numbers of particles. A water molecule has a relative mass of 18; a unit of $\ce{MgSO4}$ has 120, over 6 times as much. So nearly equal masses of salt and water hold very different numbers of particles, and only moles count them.

**Compare them:**
**1.** Masses: 2.40 g against 2.52 g, which gives nearly 1 : 1.
**2.** Moles: $0.02$ against $0.14$, which gives 1 : 7.

noteBlocks.prompt: A student divides the mass of water lost by the mass of anhydrous salt to find x. Why does this not work?
options: x is a ratio of particles, and equal masses are not equal numbers of particles
the two masses should be added, not divided
the mass of water should be divided by 16 first
noteBlocks.answer: x is a ratio of particles, and equal masses are not equal numbers of particles
noteBlocks.explain: Look at the comparison: masses of 2.40 g and 2.52 g are nearly 1 : 1, but the particles are 1 : 7, because each salt unit is much heavier than a water molecule. x counts particles, so it needs moles.

noteBlocks.md: An **empirical formula** is the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element in a compound; a **molecular formula** gives the actual number of each atom in a molecule. From masses: divide each by its Ar, then by the smallest.

**See it done**: 5.60 g of iron joined with 2.40 g of oxygen.
**1.** Fe: $5.60 \div 56 = 0.1$; O: $2.40 \div 16 = 0.15$.
**2.** Divide by the smaller: $0.15 \div 0.1 = 1.5$, so 1 : 1.5.
**3.** Double to whole numbers: 2 : 3, so $\ce{Fe2O3}$.

findTheMistake.stem:
Oisín is asked: 'Calculate the Mr of Na₂CO₃·10H₂O. [1]' (Na = 23; C = 12; O = 16; H = 1)
His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The carbonate ion has three oxygen atoms, not two: Na₂CO₃ is 2 × 23 + 12 + 3 × 16 = 106. His water and his adding are right, so the one slip costs the mark.
findTheMistake.feedback: With the third oxygen the Mr is 106 + 180 = 286. Count every atom of the salt before adding the water.

findTheMistake.stem:
Saoirse is asked to find x in MgSO₄·xH₂O: 4.92 g of the hydrate left 2.40 g at constant mass.
Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: x counts waters per salt unit, so the water's moles go on top: 0.14 ÷ 0.02 = 7. A value below 1 cannot be x, since at least one water is bonded to each unit.
findTheMistake.feedback: Her three moles lines are all right. Only the last division is upside down.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ruairí is asked: 'Describe how to heat a hydrated salt to constant mass. [2]'
His method:
studentWorking: Step 2 = add the hydrated salt and weigh again
Step 3 = heat strongly, cool, then weigh
Step 4 = weigh again until two masses are the same
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Weighing again without heating again changes nothing, so the mass cannot fall any further. Constant mass means repeating the heating and the weighing until two masses agree.
correction: Step 4 = heat, cool and weigh again until two masses are the same
findTheMistake.feedback: Steps 1 to 3 are right. Step 4 must repeat the heating too; the 2023 report found this the most common slip.

findings.asked: What water of crystallisation means, two Mr values, x from a hydrate's Mr, the masses from a heating experiment and why it was heated and weighed until two masses agreed.
findings.wentWrong: Few could define water of crystallisation; very few found x, usually from a wrong Mr for the anhydrous salt or by not dividing by 18; few could say why the heating and weighing were repeated.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Worked out the salt's Mr, took it from the total, divided by 18, and said the repeats made sure all the water had gone.
findings.rule: x = (Mr of the hydrate − Mr of the salt) ÷ 18; heat to constant mass to remove all the water.

findings.asked: What hydrated means, how to heat to constant mass, and x from the masses before and after heating.
findings.wentWrong: Few defined hydrated; few described constant mass, most often reweighing without heating again; moles were found well, but very few then reached x.
findings.rule: Heat and weigh, and repeat both; x = moles of water ÷ moles of anhydrous salt.

findings.asked: The term for a solid holding water of crystallisation, an Mr, the name of the reaction that removes the water, the method, and the dehydration equation.
findings.wentWrong: The term and thermal decomposition were not well known, nor were the evaporating dish and constant mass; in the equation the 2 in front of the water was often left out or put in front of the salt.
findings.rule: Hydrated; thermal decomposition; evaporating basin, Bunsen burner, constant mass; keep the number in front of the water.

findings.asked: A two-mark definition of water of crystallisation, the name of the reaction, and an empirical formula from masses.
findings.wentWrong: The definition was not well answered; the moles were found well, but only some reached the empirical formula.
findings.rule: Water chemically bonded into the crystal structure; empirical formula from the simplest whole-number ratio of moles.

findings.asked: The terms in a passage, the Mr of a hydrate, and a labelled diagram of the assembled apparatus for removing the water.
findings.wentWrong: The terms were well known; the Mr often lost an oxygen atom; the diagrams were poor: 3-D, instructions not followed, tripods with four legs and labels missing.
findings.rule: Count every atom before adding the water; draw a flat, assembled, labelled section.

findings.asked: The meaning of water of crystallisation.
findings.wentWrong: It was answered much better than in earlier series but still proved hard for some.
findings.rule: Water chemically bonded into the crystal structure.

findings.asked: The practical: describing hydrated magnesium sulfate, recording masses to 2 decimal places, calculating the masses, and describing the anhydrous salt.
findings.wentWrong: The practical was done well; marks were lost for masses not to 2 decimal places, for subtracting the wrong values, and occasionally for white crystals instead of a white powder.
findings.rule: Record every mass to 2 d.p.; subtract the crucible; anhydrous magnesium sulfate is a white powder.

findings.asked: The mass and moles of water lost from hydrated copper(II) sulfate, two Mr values, and the colour change on heating.
findings.wentWrong: Very few turned the mass of water into moles; the hydrate's Mr was harder than the anhydrous salt's; many colour changes were given wrongly.
findings.rule: Moles of water = mass ÷ 18; heating goes blue to white.

findings.asked: x in CuSO4.xH2O from the masses before and after heating, and the colour of the anhydrous salt.
findings.wentWrong: The moles of the anhydrous salt and x challenged some, though carried-forward marks helped; the colour was well known.
findings.rule: Salt's moles from its own Mr; x = water's moles ÷ salt's moles.

findings.asked: What colour anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns once water reaches it.
findings.wentWrong: Very few knew the anhydrous salt is white; colourless was a common wrong answer, though most knew the hydrated salt is blue.
findings.rule: White to blue: the test for water.

insight.ruleToRemember: Water of crystallisation is water chemically bonded into the crystal structure. A hydrate's Mr is the salt's plus n × 18. Heat, cool and weigh, repeating until two masses agree; then x = moles of water ÷ moles of anhydrous salt. An empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of moles.
insight.aStarSignal: Finding x from only a percentage of mass remaining, and explaining how stopping before constant mass lowers x.
